title: Does Eating Organic Make You Healthier?

scenes.purpose: Set up the two shoppers whose health the video compares.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence: the first as the shoppers are pictured, the second as the organic shopper's better health lands; "better health" turns green.
onScreenText: Organic cart or cheapest cart
Years later: better health

scenes.direction: Cold open; second line on s02.
scenes.narration: Picture a pair of shoppers: the first fills the cart with organic food, the other buys whatever is cheapest. Years later, the organic shopper is in better health.

scenes.purpose: Pose the first question: food or the person.

visual.description: The question types on, large and centred; "the kind of person" holds in amber.
onScreenText: Was it the food, or the kind of person who buys it?

scenes.direction: Hold one second after the question mark lands.
scenes.narration: Was it the food, or the kind of person who buys it?

scenes.purpose: Pose the second question the video answers.

visual.description: The second question types on in the same style; "cancer" turns amber.
onScreenText: Does organic food lower your risk of cancer?

scenes.direction: Hold half a second, then cut to the first quote.
scenes.narration: And behind that sits a second question: does organic food lower your risk of cancer?

scenes.purpose: Give the case for organic in a channel's own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "lots of health benefits" turns green.
onScreenText: "it seems to me that organic has lots of health benefits"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: The channel Seeker makes one case: "it seems to me that organic has lots of health benefits".

scenes.purpose: Show the stronger version of the claim.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "prevent" turns green.
onScreenText: "helps to prevent autoimmune and chronic diseases"

scenes.direction: Wipe from the previous quote card.
scenes.narration: Dr. Jason West goes further, saying eating organic "helps to prevent autoimmune and chronic diseases".

scenes.purpose: Give the opposing view in its own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, mirrored from the previous one; "isn't clear evidence" turns amber.
onScreenText: "there isn’t clear evidence that organic foods are also healthier for people"

scenes.direction: Wipe from the previous quote card; hold half a second before the studies.
scenes.narration: Harvard Health disagrees: "there isn’t clear evidence that organic foods are also healthier for people".

scenes.purpose: Show what the observational studies found, in the review's words.

visual.description: The review's conclusion paragraph; the list of outcomes highlights left to right as the narration names them.

excerpt.highlight: reduced incidence of metabolic syndrome, high BMI, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, infertility, birth defects

scenes.direction: Push in on the highlighted list.
scenes.narration: A systematic review found that, in observational studies, eating organic went along with lower rates of metabolic syndrome, high body weight, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, infertility and birth defects, among other outcomes.

scenes.purpose: Show the same review's warning about the people who eat organic.

visual.description: Same paragraph; the highlight moves to the sentence about healthier diets and less overweight.

excerpt.highlight: Consumption of organic food is often tied to overall healthier dietary practices and lower levels of overweight and obesity

scenes.direction: Pan down the page to the warning; no cut.
scenes.narration: The same review warns that organic eating often comes with a healthier diet overall and less overweight, and that this is likely to sway those results.

scenes.purpose: Show a second review reaching the same caution, and why.

visual.description: The second review's paragraph; the sentence saying causation cannot yet be determined highlights on s10.

excerpt.highlight: it is presently not possible to determine whether organic food plays a causal role in these observations

scenes.direction: Cut in; hold the highlight through s11.
scenes.narration: A second review saw similar signals, for childhood allergies, adult overweight and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and concluded that it is not yet possible to say whether organic food causes any of them. Its authors point out that people who prefer organic also eat more fruit, vegetables, whole grains and legumes and less meat, and they expect those people to have less diabetes and cardiovascular disease as a consequence of that diet.

scenes.purpose: Turn from observation to trials.

visual.description: The question types on centred; "trials" turns amber.
onScreenText: What about trials?

scenes.direction: Hold half a second.
scenes.narration: What about trials, where researchers change what people eat and watch what happens?

scenes.purpose: Show what the trials measured, in the review's words.

visual.description: The review's conclusion; the sentence on short trials and surrogate markers highlights.

excerpt.highlight: Clinical trial research has been short-term and measured largely surrogate markers with limited positive results.

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: Those trials have been short, and have mostly measured stand-in markers rather than disease itself, with limited positive results.

scenes.purpose: Show how few human studies looked at actual illness.

visual.description: Two horizontal bars: 17 human studies, then 3 that examined clinical outcomes; the short bar turns amber as "only 3" is said.

chart.title: Human studies in the review
chart.note: The 3 clinical studies found no significant differences; the bars count studies, not people.

scenes.direction: Bars grow in order; the second lands on "only 3".
scenes.narration: Another review counted 17 studies in people, and only 3 of them looked at actual illness: they found no significant differences in allergic conditions or in symptomatic Campylobacter infection.

scenes.purpose: Show the marker studies found nothing meaningful.

visual.description: The review's data synthesis; "did not identify clinically meaningful differences" highlights.

excerpt.highlight: did not identify clinically meaningful differences

scenes.direction: Cut in from the chart.
scenes.narration: Studies in adults that measured nutrients and other markers in blood, urine, breast milk and semen found no clinically meaningful differences.

scenes.purpose: Show the report's finding of no well-powered study.

visual.description: The report's paragraph; the phrase on studies that directly demonstrate health benefits highlights.

excerpt.highlight: human studies that directly demonstrate health benefits or disease protection

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: And a report on organic foods found no well-powered human study that directly shows a health benefit, or protection from disease, from eating an organic diet.

scenes.purpose: Give the first answer plainly.

visual.description: One line, large and centred; "not proven" holds in amber.
onScreenText: No health benefit proven in people

scenes.direction: Hold one second after the answer.
scenes.narration: So no health benefit of eating organic has been proven in the people who eat it.

scenes.purpose: Keep the door open: lower pesticide exposure might matter.

visual.description: The review's conclusion; the urinary metabolites sentence highlights first, then the sentence on possible health benefits.

excerpt.highlight: it seems possible that ongoing reduced exposure may translate to health benefits

scenes.direction: Cut in on "Not proven is not the same as ruled out".
scenes.narration: Not proven is not the same as ruled out: studies consistently find fewer pesticide breakdown products in the urine of people on an organic diet, and the first review's authors think it possible that lower exposure, kept up over time, could turn into health benefits.

scenes.purpose: Hand over to the cancer question.

visual.description: The question types on centred; "cancer" turns amber.
onScreenText: Who gets cancer?

scenes.direction: Hold one second before the second question.
scenes.narration: If a benefit is there, could it show up in the outcome people fear most: who gets cancer?

scenes.purpose: Give the cancer claim in its maker's words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "about 25 percent" turns green.
onScreenText: "the organic food group were protected by about 25 percent"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: Tim Spector, on the ZOE channel, says one study found "the organic food group were protected by about 25 percent".

scenes.purpose: Give the opposing study as a cancer centre describes it.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, mirrored; "not associated" turns amber.
onScreenText: "organic food intake was not associated with a decreased cancer risk for the cancers that they evaluated"

scenes.direction: Wipe from the previous quote card.
scenes.narration: A Dana-Farber Cancer Institute video describes a large study of British women that found "organic food intake was not associated with a decreased cancer risk for the cancers that they evaluated".

scenes.purpose: Put the French cohort's size next to its absolute difference.

visual.description: Two tiles: 68,946 adults on s22, then the 0.6% absolute difference on s23, the second in amber.

chart.title: NutriNet-Santé cohort
chart.note: The narrated drop is relative (top vs bottom quarter, HR 0.75); the 0.6% is the absolute risk reduction. Observational, not a trial.

scenes.direction: First tile on s22, second on "0.6 percent"; hold half a second.
scenes.narration: The NutriNet-Santé cohort followed 68,946 adults for an average of 4.6 years, and after adjusting for other factors, the quarter who scored highest for eating organic had a 25 percent lower rate of cancer than the quarter who scored lowest. In absolute terms, though, the difference in the share of people who got cancer was 0.6 percent.

scenes.purpose: Show which cancers the lower risk covered.

visual.description: The review's summary of the French cohort; the cancer types highlight.

excerpt.highlight: postmenopausal breast cancer, with no association for other types of cancer

scenes.direction: Cut in.
scenes.narration: The lower risk showed up for non-Hodgkin lymphoma and postmenopausal breast cancer, and not for other types of cancer.

scenes.purpose: Show the British cohort's overall result.

visual.description: The Million Women Study abstract; the finding of no reduction in all cancer highlights.

excerpt.highlight: Consumption of organic food was not associated with a reduction in the incidence of all cancer

citations.label: Bradbury et al. 2014, Million Women Study

scenes.direction: Hard cut in on "United Kingdom".
scenes.narration: In the United Kingdom, the Million Women Study followed its participants for about 9 years. Women who said they usually or always ate organic had no lower rate of cancer overall than women who said they never did, and a slightly higher rate of breast cancer.

scenes.purpose: Show the authors hedging even the lymphoma result.

visual.description: Same abstract; the highlight moves to the conclusion's hedge.

citations.label: Bradbury et al. 2014, Million Women Study

scenes.direction: Pan to the conclusion; no cut.
scenes.narration: The one cancer that was lower was non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and the authors' conclusion hedges even that: "except possibly for non-Hodgkin lymphoma".

scenes.purpose: Set the two cohorts side by side.

visual.description: Two lines: lymphoma in green, breast cancer in amber.
onScreenText: Lymphoma: they agree
Breast cancer: opposite directions

scenes.direction: Both lines on the sentence; hold.
scenes.narration: So these cohorts agree on lymphoma and point in opposite directions on breast cancer.

scenes.purpose: Ask why.

visual.description: The question types on centred.
onScreenText: Why would the cohorts disagree?

scenes.direction: Hold half a second.
scenes.narration: Why would the cohorts disagree?

scenes.purpose: Show who the French organic eaters were.

visual.description: The French paper's paragraph; the list of traits highlights as each is named.

excerpt.highlight: positively associated with female sex, high occupational status or monthly income per household unit, postsecondary graduate educational level, physical activity

scenes.direction: Cut in.
scenes.narration: In NutriNet-Santé, the higher people scored for eating organic, the more likely they were to be women, better paid, better educated and physically active, and the more fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes and the less meat they ate.

scenes.purpose: Show who the British organic eaters were.

visual.description: The British paper's paragraph; exercise, smoking and meat highlight.

excerpt.highlight: more likely to report that they participated in strenuous physical activity, and were less likely to smoke or eat red and processed meat

citations.label: Bradbury et al. 2014, Million Women Study

scenes.direction: Wipe from the previous excerpt.
scenes.narration: In the British study, women who usually or always ate organic were more likely to report strenuous exercise and less likely to smoke or eat red and processed meat, though differences in socioeconomic status were smaller.

scenes.purpose: Show why adjusting for diet may not settle it.

visual.description: The review's paragraph on diet adjustment; the sentence on diet quality highlights.

excerpt.highlight: It is possible that the benefit observed for organic intake may be partly due to the quality and composition of the diet rather than a direct effect of organic food consumption.

scenes.direction: Cut in on "the systematic review from earlier".
scenes.narration: The French team found that adding more diet measures did not change its result, but the systematic review from earlier notes that studies adjust for diet in different ways, so a benefit may still be partly down to whole-food diets and healthier lives rather than the organic food itself.

scenes.purpose: Give the second answer plainly.

visual.description: Two lines: the British cohort's result, then the French cohort's; "small absolute difference" in amber.
onScreenText: One cohort: no overall drop
The other: a small absolute difference

scenes.direction: Hold one second after the answer.
scenes.narration: So the evidence does not show that organic food lowers cancer risk: one cohort found no overall drop, and the other found a small absolute difference among people who also ate and lived differently.

scenes.purpose: Give the viewer the question to carry away.

visual.description: The question types on centred; "given" and "chose" turn amber.
onScreenText: Given the food, or chose it?

scenes.direction: Hold half a second.
scenes.narration: So the next time a label or a video promises that organic food will keep you well, ask one question: was the benefit measured in people who were given the food, or in people who chose it?

scenes.purpose: Add the follow-up questions.

visual.description: Two short lines build; hold to the end card.
onScreenText: An illness or a number on a blood test
For how long

scenes.direction: Hold one second, fade out.
scenes.narration: Then ask what was counted, an illness or a number on a blood test, and for how long.
